claim: The synaptic connection from medial habenula (MHb) to interpeduncular nucleus (IPN) is critical for emotion-related behaviors.
source: The synaptic connection from medial habenula (MHb) to interpeduncular nucleus (IPN) is critical for emotion-related behaviors and uniquely expresses R-type Ca2+ channels (Cav2.3) and auxiliary GABAB receptor (GBR) subunits, the K+-channel tetramerization domain-containing proteins (KCTDs).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature establishing the behavioral relevance of this pathway.

claim: The MHb-IPN pathway uniquely expresses R-type Ca2+ channels (Cav2.3).
source: The synaptic connection from medial habenula (MHb) to interpeduncular nucleus (IPN) is critical for emotion-related behaviors and uniquely expresses R-type Ca2+ channels (Cav2.3) and auxiliary GABAB receptor (GBR) subunits, the K+-channel tetramerization domain-containing proteins (KCTDs).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's own data and previous literature.

claim: The MHb-IPN pathway uniquely expresses auxiliary GABAB receptor (GBR) subunits, the K+-channel tetramerization domain-containing proteins (KCTDs).
source: The synaptic connection from medial habenula (MHb) to interpeduncular nucleus (IPN) is critical for emotion-related behaviors and uniquely expresses R-type Ca2+ channels (Cav2.3) and auxiliary GABAB receptor (GBR) subunits, the K+-channel tetramerization domain-containing proteins (KCTDs).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's own data showing unique expression patterns of KCTDs in this pathway.

claim: Activation of GBRs facilitates transmitter release from MHb terminals in the rostral IPN.
source: Activation of GBRs facilitates or inhibits transmitter release from MHb terminals depending on the IPN subnucleus, but the role of KCTDs is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing baclofen-mediated potentiation of EPSCs in rostral IPN neurons.

claim: Activation of GBRs inhibits transmitter release from MHb terminals in the lateral IPN.
source: Activation of GBRs facilitates or inhibits transmitter release from MHb terminals depending on the IPN subnucleus, but the role of KCTDs is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing baclofen-mediated reduction of EPSCs in lateral IPN neurons.

claim: KCTD8 and KCTD12b directly bind to Cav2.3 in heterologous cells.
source: We show in heterologous cells that KCTD8 and KCTD12b directly bind to Cav2.3 and that KCTD8 potentiates Cav2.3 currents in the absence of GBRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in HEK293T cells.

claim: KCTD8 potentiates Cav2.3 currents in the absence of GBRs in heterologous cells.
source: We show in heterologous cells that KCTD8 and KCTD12b directly bind to Cav2.3 and that KCTD8 potentiates Cav2.3 currents in the absence of GBRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell recordings from HEK293 cells showing increased current densities with KCTD8 co-expression.

claim: In the rostral IPN, KCTD8, KCTD12b, and Cav2.3 co-localize at the presynaptic active zone.
source: In the rostral IPN, KCTD8, KCTD12b, and Cav2.3 co-localize at the presynaptic active zone.
evidence: This claim is supported by SDS-FRL electron microscopy data showing co-localization of these proteins.

claim: Genetic deletion of KCTD8 or KCTD12b modulates Cav2.3-mediated release bidirectionally.
source: Genetic deletion indicated a bidirectional modulation of Cav2.3-mediated release by these KCTDs with a compensatory increase of KCTD8 in the active zone in KCTD12b-deficient mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by paired-pulse ratio and variance-mean analysis in KCTD knockout mice.

claim: KCTD12b-deficient mice show a compensatory increase of KCTD8 in the active zone.
source: Genetic deletion indicated a bidirectional modulation of Cav2.3-mediated release by these KCTDs with a compensatory increase of KCTD8 in the active zone in KCTD12b-deficient mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by SDS-FRL data showing increased KCTD8 density in the active zone of KCTD12b KO mice.

claim: The interaction of Cav2.3 with KCTDs scales synaptic strength independent of GBR activation.
source: The interaction of Cav2.3 with KCTDs therefore scales synaptic strength independent of GBR activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that KCTD deletion affects basal release probability without affecting GBR-mediated potentiation.

claim: The dorsal MHb projects to the lateral IPN.
source: The medial habenula (MHb) is an epithalamic structure that exclusively projects to the interpeduncular nucleus (IPN), with the dorsal MHb projecting to the lateral IPN and the ventral MHb projecting to the rostral and central subnuclei of the IPN (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data and Figure 1A showing the projection patterns.

claim: The ventral MHb projects to the rostral and central subnuclei of the IPN.
source: The medial habenula (MHb) is an epithalamic structure that exclusively projects to the interpeduncular nucleus (IPN), with the dorsal MHb projecting to the lateral IPN and the ventral MHb projecting to the rostral and central subnuclei of the IPN (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data and Figure 1A showing the projection patterns.

claim: The MHb-IPN pathway is involved in nicotine addiction and aversion.
source: This pathway is involved in various behaviors, including nicotine addiction and aversion (Agetsuma et al., 2010; Koppensteiner et al., 2016; Koppensteiner et al., 2017; Melani et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2016; Zhao-Shea et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Cav2.3 is prominently localized presynaptically in the IPN.
source: A striking property of the MHb-IPN pathway is the prominent presynaptic localization of the R-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channel 2.3 (Cav2.3), a channel mainly located in postsynaptic elements in other brain areas (Parajuli et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and confirmed by the manuscript's own immunofluorescence and electron microscopy data.

claim: Cav2.3 is mainly located in postsynaptic elements in other brain areas.
source: A striking property of the MHb-IPN pathway is the prominent presynaptic localization of the R-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channel 2.3 (Cav2.3), a channel mainly located in postsynaptic elements in other brain areas (Parajuli et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Activation of presynaptic GABAB receptors on MHb terminals increases neurotransmitter release up to 10-fold in the ventral MHb to rostral/central IPN pathway.
source: Furthermore, activation of presynaptic GABAB receptors (GBRs) on MHb terminals exerts an unusual facilitatory effect by increasing neurotransmitter release up to 10-fold (Zhang et al., 2016), and this effect appears to be involved in synaptic plasticity (Koppensteiner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and confirmed by the manuscript's own data.

claim: GBR-mediated potentiation is involved in synaptic plasticity at the MHb-IPN pathway.
source: Furthermore, activation of presynaptic GABAB receptors (GBRs) on MHb terminals exerts an unusual facilitatory effect by increasing neurotransmitter release up to 10-fold (Zhang et al., 2016), and this effect appears to be involved in synaptic plasticity (Koppensteiner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In the glutamatergic/substance-P-ergic pathway from the dorsal MHb to the lateral IPN, release is attenuated by GBR activation.
source: Interestingly, this potentiation via presynaptic GBR activation only occurs in the glutamatergic/cholinergic pathway from the ventral MHb to the rostral/central IPN, whereas in the glutamatergic/substance-P-ergic pathway from the dorsal MHb to the lateral IPN, the release is attenuated by GBR activation (Melani et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and confirmed by the manuscript's own data.

claim: GBRs are ubiquitously expressed in MHb-IPN pathways.
source: Although GBRs are ubiquitously expressed in these MHb-IPN pathways (Margeta-Mitrovic et al., 1999), the presynaptic localization and function of their auxiliary KCTD subunits is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and confirmed by the manuscript's immunofluorescence data.

claim: Four KCTD subunits (KCTD8, 12, 12b, and 16) serve as GBR auxiliary subunits in the brain.
source: Four KCTD subunits, KCTD8, 12, 12b, and 16, serve as GBR auxiliary subunits in the brain (Schwenk et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: KCTD subunits bind as hetero- and homo-pentamers to GBRs.
source: KCTD subunits bind as hetero- and homo-pentamers to GBRs and modulate their signaling kinetics (Fritzius et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: KCTD subunits modulate GBR signaling kinetics.
source: KCTD subunits bind as hetero- and homo-pentamers to GBRs and modulate their signaling kinetics (Fritzius et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The T1 domain of KCTD subunits binds to the GABAB2 subunit.
source: The T1 domain binds to the GABAB2 subunit, while the H1 domain binds to the Gβ subunit of the guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G-protein) (Schwenk et al., 2010; Turecek et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The H1 domain of KCTD subunits binds to the Gβ subunit of the G-protein.
source: The T1 domain binds to the GABAB2 subunit, while the H1 domain binds to the Gβ subunit of the guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G-protein) (Schwenk et al., 2010; Turecek et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: KCTD8 and 16 encode a C-terminal H2 domain, while KCTD12 and 12b do not.
source: KCTD8 and 16, but not KCTD12 and 12b, additionally encode a C-terminal H2 domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural knowledge of KCTD proteins.

claim: The absence of the H2 domain enables KCTD12 and 12b to rapidly desensitize GBR responses by uncoupling the Gβγ subunits of the G-protein from effector channels.
source: The absence of the H2 domain enables KCTD12 and 12b to rapidly desensitize GBR responses by uncoupling the Gβγ subunits of the G-protein from effector channels (Turecek et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: KCTD12 and 12b can form hetero-pentamers with each other and with KCTD8 and 16.
source: KCTD12 and 12b can form hetero-pentamers with each other but also with KCTD8 and 16 (Fritzius et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: KCTD8 is exclusively and strongly expressed in MHb and, to a lesser extent, IPN neurons, with the exception of weak expression in the cerebellum and superior colliculus.
source: With the exception of a weak expression in the cerebellum and superior colliculus, KCTD8 is exclusively and strongly expressed in MHb and, to a lesser extent, IPN neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and confirmed by the manuscript's immunofluorescence data.

claim: KCTD12b is exclusively expressed in the ventral part of the MHb.
source: Furthermore, KCTD12b is exclusively expressed in the ventral part of the MHb (Metz et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and confirmed by the manuscript's immunofluorescence data.

claim: KCTD12 is weakly expressed in the ventral part of the MHb.
source: In contrast, KCTD12 is weakly expressed in the ventral part of the MHb, while KCTD16 is expressed in most brain areas but not the MHb.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's immunofluorescence data.

claim: KCTD16 is expressed in most brain areas but not the MHb.
source: In contrast, KCTD12 is weakly expressed in the ventral part of the MHb, while KCTD16 is expressed in most brain areas but not the MHb.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of KCTD expression patterns.

claim: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels co-precipitate GBRs and their auxiliary KCTD subunits together with release machinery proteins of the presynaptic active zone.
source: Based on proteomics studies, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels co-precipitate GBRs and their auxiliary KCTD subunits together with release machinery proteins of the presynaptic active zone, including SNAP-25, synaptotagmins, synaptobrevin-2, Munc13-1, syntaxins, RIM1, and synapsins, among others (Müller et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous proteomics study.

claim: KCTD8 and KCTD16 co-purify with presynaptic Cav2.2 Ca2+ channels.
source: Furthermore, KCTD8 and KCTD16 were consistently found to co-purify with presynaptic Cav2.2 Ca2+ channels (Müller et al., 2010; Schwenk et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cav2.3 is located in the presynaptic active zone of habenular terminals.
source: Our results demonstrate that Cav2.3 is located in the presynaptic active zone of habenular terminals and required for fast neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's electron microscopy data.

claim: Cav2.3 is required for fast neurotransmitter release from habenular terminals.
source: Our results demonstrate that Cav2.3 is located in the presynaptic active zone of habenular terminals and required for fast neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's electrophysiology data showing strong reduction of EPSCs by SNX-482 and absence of responses in Cav2.3 KO mice.

claim: KCTD8 and KCTD12b bind to Cav2.3 at the plasma membrane in heterologous cells.
source: In heterologous cells, we found that KCTD8 and KCTD12b, but not KCTD12, bind to Cav2.3 at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments using plasma membrane extracts.

claim: KCTD12 does not bind to Cav2.3 in heterologous cells.
source: In heterologous cells, we found that KCTD8 and KCTD12b, but not KCTD12, bind to Cav2.3 at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing no binding of KCTD12 to Cav2.3.

claim: Cav2.3 currents are enhanced by co-expression of KCTD8 in the absence of GBRs.
source: Furthermore, Cav2.3 currents were enhanced by co-expression of KCTD8, but not KCTD12b in the absence of GBRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell recordings from HEK293 cells showing increased current densities with KCTD8 co-expression.

claim: Cav2.3 currents are not enhanced by co-expression of KCTD12b in the absence of GBRs.
source: Furthermore, Cav2.3 currents were enhanced by co-expression of KCTD8, but not KCTD12b in the absence of GBRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell recordings from HEK293 cells showing no change in current densities with KCTD12b co-expression.

claim: Genetic deletion of KCTD8 reduces the probability of neurotransmitter release in the ventral MHb to rostral IPN pathway.
source: Strikingly, genetic deletion of KCTD8 or KCTD12b reduced or increased, respectively, the probability of neurotransmitter release in the ventral MHb to the rostral IPN pathway without affecting GBR-mediated potentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by variance-mean analysis showing reduced release probability in KCTD8 KO mice.

claim: Genetic deletion of KCTD12b increases the probability of neurotransmitter release in the ventral MHb to rostral IPN pathway.
source: Strikingly, genetic deletion of KCTD8 or KCTD12b reduced or increased, respectively, the probability of neurotransmitter release in the ventral MHb to the rostral IPN pathway without affecting GBR-mediated potentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by variance-mean analysis showing increased release probability in KCTD12b KO mice.

claim: Genetic deletion of KCTD8 or KCTD12b does not affect GBR-mediated potentiation.
source: Strikingly, genetic deletion of KCTD8 or KCTD12b reduced or increased, respectively, the probability of neurotransmitter release in the ventral MHb to the rostral IPN pathway without affecting GBR-mediated potentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by baclofen application experiments showing similar potentiation in all KCTD KO lines.

claim: The increase of release in KCTD12b KO mice is accompanied by a compensatory recruitment of KCTD8 into the active zone.
source: The increase of release in KCTD12b knock-out (KO) mice was accompanied by a compensatory recruitment of KCTD8 into the active zone, where it closely associates with Cav2.3.
evidence: This claim is supported by SDS-FRL data showing increased KCTD8 density in the active zone of KCTD12b KO mice.

claim: In KCTD12b KO mice, KCTD8 closely associates with Cav2.3 in the active zone.
source: The increase of release in KCTD12b knock-out (KO) mice was accompanied by a compensatory recruitment of KCTD8 into the active zone, where it closely associates with Cav2.3.
evidence: This claim is supported by steric hindrance experiments showing reduced Cav2.3 labeling after KCTD8 antibody pre-incubation.

claim: Viral expression of KCTD12b in MHb neurons reduces the increased release probability in KCTD12b KO mice.
source: Furthermore, viral expression of KCTD12b in MHb neurons reduced the increased release probability in KCTD12b KO mice, whereas overexpression of KCTD8 in MHb neurons of wild-type mice increased release probability.
evidence: This claim is supported by paired-pulse ratio measurements in lentivirus-injected mice.

claim: Overexpression of KCTD8 in MHb neurons of wild-type mice increases release probability.
source: Furthermore, viral expression of KCTD12b in MHb neurons reduced the increased release probability in KCTD12b KO mice, whereas overexpression of KCTD8 in MHb neurons of wild-type mice increased release probability.
evidence: This claim is supported by paired-pulse ratio measurements in lentivirus-injected mice.

claim: Synaptic strength at the MHb-IPN pathway is scaled via GBR-independent Cav2.3–KCTD interactions in the presynaptic active zone.
source: These results support that synaptic strength at the MHb-IPN pathway is scaled via GBR-independent Cav2.3–KCTD interactions in the presynaptic active zone.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined results showing KCTD modulation of release independent of GBR activation.

claim: GBR activation facilitates electrically evoked neurotransmitter release in the ventral MHb-rostral/central IPN pathway.
source: GBR activation has been reported to facilitate both electrically and optogenetically evoked neurotransmitter release in the ventral MHb-rostral/central IPN pathway (Koppensteiner et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016), whereas it inhibits release in the dorsal MHb-lateral IPN (Melani et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by the manuscript's own data.

claim: GBR activation facilitates optogenetically evoked neurotransmitter release in the ventral MHb-rostral/central IPN pathway.
source: GBR activation has been reported to facilitate both electrically and optogenetically evoked neurotransmitter release in the ventral MHb-rostral/central IPN pathway (Koppensteiner et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016), whereas it inhibits release in the dorsal MHb-lateral IPN (Melani et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Baclofen at 1 µM produces a strong increase in EPSC amplitudes in rostral IPN neurons.
source: We confirmed that rostral IPN neurons exhibit a strong increase in excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) amplitudes following GBR activation with 1 µM baclofen (Figure 1C), whereas EPSC amplitudes were reduced by baclofen in lateral IPN neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Baclofen at 1 µM reduces EPSC amplitudes in lateral IPN neurons.
source: We confirmed that rostral IPN neurons exhibit a strong increase in excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) amplitudes following GBR activation with 1 µM baclofen (Figure 1C), whereas EPSC amplitudes were reduced by baclofen in lateral IPN neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SNX-482 at 1 µM strongly reduces the amplitude of EPSCs by 83% in rostral IPN neurons.
source: In rostral and lateral IPN neurons, 1 µM SNX-482 strongly reduced the amplitude of EPSCs by 83% and 52%, respectively (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: SNX-482 at 1 µM reduces the amplitude of EPSCs by 52% in lateral IPN neurons.
source: In rostral and lateral IPN neurons, 1 µM SNX-482 strongly reduced the amplitude of EPSCs by 83% and 52%, respectively (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The SNX-482-mediated reduction in EPSC amplitudes is significantly stronger in the ventral MHb to rostral IPN pathway compared to the dorsal MHb to lateral IPN pathway.
source: The SNX-482-mediated reduction in EPSC amplitudes was significantly stronger in the ventral MHb to rostral IPN pathway compared to the dorsal MHb to lateral IPN pathway (main effect of IPN subnucleus F1, 395 = 213.7, p<0.0001; two-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the manuscript's electrophysiology data.

claim: SNX-482 does not significantly affect action potential peak times in ventral MHb neurons.
source: In addition, SNX-482 did not significantly affect action potential peak times or full-widths at half maximum in ventral MHb neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; peak times: control: 0.86 ± 0.03 ms, n = 3; SNX-482: 0.93 ± 0.05 ms, n = 4; t5 = 1.083, p=0.3282; full-widths: control 1.08 ± 0.07 ms, n = 3; SNX-482: 1.06 ± 0.03 ms, n = 4, t5 = 0.3852, p=0.7159; unpaired t-test), suggesting that the reduction of neurotransmitter release by SNX-482 was not caused by a blockade of voltage-gated Na+ or K+ channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SNX-482 does not significantly affect action potential full-widths at half maximum in ventral MHb neurons.
source: In addition, SNX-482 did not significantly affect action potential peak times or full-widths at half maximum in ventral MHb neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; peak times: control: 0.86 ± 0.03 ms, n = 3; SNX-482: 0.93 ± 0.05 ms, n = 4; t5 = 1.083, p=0.3282; full-widths: control 1.08 ± 0.07 ms, n = 3; SNX-482: 1.06 ± 0.03 ms, n = 4, t5 = 0.3852, p=0.7159; unpaired t-test), suggesting that the reduction of neurotransmitter release by SNX-482 was not caused by a blockade of voltage-gated Na+ or K+ channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The reduction of neurotransmitter release by SNX-482 is not caused by a blockade of voltage-gated Na+ or K+ channels.
source: In addition, SNX-482 did not significantly affect action potential peak times or full-widths at half maximum in ventral MHb neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; peak times: control: 0.86 ± 0.03 ms, n = 3; SNX-482: 0.93 ± 0.05 ms, n = 4; t5 = 1.083, p=0.3282; full-widths: control 1.08 ± 0.07 ms, n = 3; SNX-482: 1.06 ± 0.03 ms, n = 4, t5 = 0.3852, p=0.7159; unpaired t-test), suggesting that the reduction of neurotransmitter release by SNX-482 was not caused by a blockade of voltage-gated Na+ or K+ channels.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the lack of effect of SNX-482 on action potential properties.

claim: In Cav2.3 KO mice, 10 Hz electrical stimulation for 1 s fails to evoke synaptic responses in rostral IPN neurons.
source: Applying these criteria, 10 Hz electrical stimulation for 1 s failed to evoke synaptic responses in the nine of nine recorded rostral IPN neurons (Figure 1H,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1H,J.

claim: In Cav2.3 KO mice, seven of nine recorded lateral IPN neurons show EPSC responses to 10 Hz electrical stimulation.
source: In contrast, seven of nine recorded lateral IPN neurons showed EPSC responses (Figure 1I,J; main effect of IPN subnucleus: F1, 160 = 120.4, p<0.0001; two-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1I,J.

claim: Ventral MHb terminals in the rostral IPN rely exclusively on Cav2.3 for release.
source: Overall, these results suggest that ventral MHb terminals in the rostral IPN rely exclusively on Cav2.3 for release, whereas dorsal MHb terminals in the lateral IPN rely on Cav2.3 and additional Ca2+ channels.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the complete absence of responses in Cav2.3 KO mice and strong SNX-482 effect.

claim: Dorsal MHb terminals in the lateral IPN rely on Cav2.3 and additional Ca2+ channels.
source: Overall, these results suggest that ventral MHb terminals in the rostral IPN rely exclusively on Cav2.3 for release, whereas dorsal MHb terminals in the lateral IPN rely on Cav2.3 and additional Ca2+ channels.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the partial responses remaining in Cav2.3 KO mice and partial SNX-482 effect.

claim: ω-conotoxin GVIA does not reduce EPSC amplitudes further after SNX-482 application in lateral IPN neurons.
source: While SNX-482 produced a similar decrease in EPSC amplitude as in the optogenetic stimulation experiment (Figure 1K,L, effect of electrical vs. optogenetic stimulation: F1, 305 = 1.830, p=0.1772; main effect of SNX: F23, 305 = 17.41, p<0.0001; Interaction F23, 305 = 1.842, p>0.9999, two-way ANOVA of time courses between minutes 0–25), ω-conotoxin did not reduce EPSC amplitudes further.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The remaining EPSC amplitude after SNX-482 and ω-conotoxin application is completely blocked by CdCl2 in lateral IPN neurons.
source: The remaining EPSC amplitude was completely blocked by CdCl2, suggesting an involvement of either P/Q- or L-type Ca2+ channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Dorsal MHb terminals likely express Cav2.3 together with P/Q- or L-type Ca2+ channels.
source: Therefore, dorsal MHb terminals likely express Cav2.3 together with other Ca2+ channels, potentially L-type Ca2+ channels.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the pharmacological profile of remaining currents after SNX-482 and ω-conotoxin.

claim: KCTD8 immunofluorescence is strong in all IPN subnuclei.
source: Immunoreactivity for KCTD8 appeared strong in all IPN subnuclei (Figure 2A), consistent with its strong expression throughout MHb and presynaptic localization in IPN.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: KCTD12 immunofluorescence is strong in the rostral and central subnuclei but faint in the lateral subnucleus.
source: KCTD12 immunofluorescence appeared strong in the rostral and central subnuclei but faint in the lateral subnucleus (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: KCTD12b immunoreactivity is only present in the rostral and central but not the lateral IPN subnuclei.
source: In contrast, immunoreactivity for KCTD12b was only present in the rostral and central but not the lateral IPN subnuclei, indicating its absence in the dorsal MHb-IPN pathway (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: KCTD12b is absent in the dorsal MHb-IPN pathway.
source: In contrast, immunoreactivity for KCTD12b was only present in the rostral and central but not the lateral IPN subnuclei, indicating its absence in the dorsal MHb-IPN pathway (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the absence of KCTD12b immunoreactivity in the lateral IPN.

claim: KCTD12 immunofluorescence patterns in the rostral region suggest a mostly postsynaptic expression.
source: While KCTD12 immunofluorescence patterns in the rostral region suggested a mostly postsynaptic expression, KCTD12b signal showed the characteristic pattern of cholinergic MHb axons inside the rostral/central IPN, suggesting presynaptic expression.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the immunofluorescence pattern observed.

claim: KCTD12b signal shows the characteristic pattern of cholinergic MHb axons inside the rostral/central IPN, suggesting presynaptic expression.
source: While KCTD12 immunofluorescence patterns in the rostral region suggested a mostly postsynaptic expression, KCTD12b signal showed the characteristic pattern of cholinergic MHb axons inside the rostral/central IPN, suggesting presynaptic expression.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the immunofluorescence pattern observed.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of Cav2.3 co-precipitates KCTD8 in HEK293T cells.
source: Immunoprecipitation of Cav2.3 co-precipitated KCTD8 and KCTD12b, but not KCTD12.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of Cav2.3 co-precipitates KCTD12b in HEK293T cells.
source: Immunoprecipitation of Cav2.3 co-precipitated KCTD8 and KCTD12b, but not KCTD12.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of Cav2.3 does not co-precipitate KCTD12 in HEK293T cells.
source: Immunoprecipitation of Cav2.3 co-precipitated KCTD8 and KCTD12b, but not KCTD12.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: KCTD8 and KCTD12b are highly and similarly enriched in plasma membrane extracts compared to total membrane extracts in HEK293T cells co-expressing Cav2.3 and KCTDs.
source: Plasma membrane preparations (see Materials and methods) revealed that in HEK293T cells co-expressing Cav2.3 and KCTDs, both KCTD8 and KCTD12b are highly and similarly enriched in plasma membrane extracts, when compared to total membrane extracts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; KCTD8: 10.7-fold [±1.9], KCTD12b: 12.7-fold [±2.6], no significant difference between KCTD8 and KCTD12b, p=0.34, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's plasma membrane preparation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: KCTD8 associates with Cav2.3 at the plasma membrane in HEK293T cells.

claim: KCTD12b associates with Cav2.3 at the plasma membrane in HEK293T cells.

claim: KCTD8 and KCTD12b in MHb-derived axon terminals may directly interact with presynaptic Cav2.3, even in the absence of GBRs.

claim: The current density-to-voltage relationship shows a significant difference between KCTD8 and both Control- and KCTD12b-transfected cells.

claim: The interaction of Cav2.3 with KCTD12b does not increase the current through Cav2.3 in heterologous cells.
source: These results suggest that the interaction of Cav2.3 with KCTD8, but not KCTD12b, increases the current through Cav2.3 in heterologous cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the electrophysiology data showing no change in currents with KCTD12b co-expression.

claim: Immunogold particles for Cav2.3 are concentrated in the active zone and, to a lesser extent, the immediate peri-synaptic region.
source: Immunogold particles for Cav2.3 were concentrated in the active zone and, to a lesser extent, the immediate peri-synaptic region (Figure 3A).

claim: KCTD12 and KCTD12b labeling is detected only in MHb terminals in the rostral but not lateral IPN subnuclei.

claim: KCTD12 particles are found mostly on the postsynaptic side of asymmetrical synapses.
source: In addition, particles for KCTD12 were found mostly on the postsynaptic side of asymmetrical synapses and only few synapses exhibited presynaptic KCTD12 labeling along synaptic and extrasynaptic membrane (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Only few synapses exhibit presynaptic KCTD12 labeling along synaptic and extrasynaptic membrane.
source: In addition, particles for KCTD12 were found mostly on the postsynaptic side of asymmetrical synapses and only few synapses exhibited presynaptic KCTD12 labeling along synaptic and extrasynaptic membrane (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's pre-embedding immunogold labeling data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In MHb terminals in the rostral IPN, Cav2.3 and KCTD12b show similar localization patterns, with peak particle densities in the active zone and a gradual decrease in density with increased distance from the active zone.
source: In MHb terminals in the rostral IPN, Cav2.3 and KCTD12b showed similar localization patterns, with peak particle densities in the active zone and a gradual decrease in density with increased distance from the active zone (Figure 3A,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's pre-embedding immunogold labeling data shown in Figure 3A,E.

claim: GABAB1, KCTD8, and KCTD12 show peak localization in the peri-synaptic region with lower particle densities inside the active zone.
source: In contrast, GABAB1, KCTD8, and KCTD12 showed peak localization in the peri-synaptic region with lower particle densities inside the active zone (Figure 3B–D).

claim: KCTD12b prominently localizes to the active zone of ventral MHb terminals in the rostral IPN.
source: These results suggest that KCTD12b prominently localized to the active zone of ventral MHb terminals in the rostral IPN, whereas KCTD8 dominates the active zone of dorsal MHb terminals in the lateral IPN (Figure 3F).

claim: KCTD8 dominates the active zone of dorsal MHb terminals in the lateral IPN.
source: These results suggest that KCTD12b prominently localized to the active zone of ventral MHb terminals in the rostral IPN, whereas KCTD8 dominates the active zone of dorsal MHb terminals in the lateral IPN (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the pre-embedding immunogold labeling data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Gold particles for Cav2.3 are detected on the P-face of the presynaptic active zone in SDS-FRL.
source: We detected gold particles for Cav2.3 on the P-face of the presynaptic active zone and confirmed antibody specificity using Cav2.3 KO mice (Figure 4B,C,F; average density WT: 147.8 ± 23.9 particles/µm², n = 4 replicas; KO: 3.4 ± 0.99 particles/µm², n = 4 replicas; WT vs. KO: t3 = 5.87, p=0.0099, paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's SDS-FRL data shown in Figure 4B,C,F.

claim: Antibody specificity for Cav2.3 is confirmed using Cav2.3 KO mice.
source: We detected gold particles for Cav2.3 on the P-face of the presynaptic active zone and confirmed antibody specificity using Cav2.3 KO mice (Figure 4B,C,F; average density WT: 147.8 ± 23.9 particles/µm², n = 4 replicas; KO: 3.4 ± 0.99 particles/µm², n = 4 replicas; WT vs. KO: t3 = 5.87, p=0.0099, paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's SDS-FRL data comparing WT and Cav2.3 KO mice shown in Figure 4B,C,F.

claim: Cav2.3 is concentrated within the active zone as confirmed by co-immunolabelings with active zone marker proteins.
source: In addition, we confirmed the concentrated localization of Cav2.3 within the active zone using co-immunolabelings with a mixture of antibodies against marker proteins for the active zone, RIM1/2, neurexin, and CAST (Figure 4D; Miki et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's SDS-FRL data with active zone marker co-labeling shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In ventral MHb terminals in the rostral IPN, Cav2.3 is co-localized with GABAB1, KCTD8, and KCTD12b in over 97% of all Cav2.3-positive active zones.
source: We found that in ventral MHb terminals in the rostral IPN, Cav2.3 is co-localized with GABAB1, KCTD8, and KCTD12b in over 97% of all Cav2.3-positive active zones (Figure 5A,B; GABAB1: 98 ± 0.70%, n = 3 replicas; KCTD8: 98 ± 1.10%, n = 3 replicas; KCTD12b: 97 ± 1.8%, n = 4 replicas).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's SDS-FRL double labeling data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Similar co-localization patterns are seen in dorsal MHb terminals located inside the lateral IPN, with the exception of an absence of KCTD12b.
source: Similar co-localization patterns were seen in dorsal MHb terminals located inside the lateral IPN (Figure 5A,B; GABAB1: 99 ± 0.69%, n = 3 replicas; KCTD8: 97 ± 0.57%, n = 3 replicas), with the exception of an absence of KCTD12b.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's SDS-FRL double labeling data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Particle numbers and densities of all tested molecules, except KCTD12b, are comparable between MHb terminals in the rostral and lateral IPN.
source: Particle numbers and densities of all tested molecules, except KCTD12b, were comparable between MHb terminals in the rostral and lateral IPN (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's SDS-FRL quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The nearest-neighbor distances (NND) of all tested molecules are significantly smaller than those obtained from simulations of randomly distributed particles.
source: In addition, the nearest-neighbor distances (NND) of all tested molecules were significantly smaller than those obtained from simulations of randomly distributed particles (Figure 5C), suggesting that Cav2.3, GABAB1, and KCTDs are clustered inside the active zone.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's NND analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Cav2.3, GABAB1, and KCTDs are clustered inside the active zone.
source: In addition, the nearest-neighbor distances (NND) of all tested molecules were significantly smaller than those obtained from simulations of randomly distributed particles (Figure 5C), suggesting that Cav2.3, GABAB1, and KCTDs are clustered inside the active zone.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the NND analysis showing smaller distances than random distribution.

claim: PPR is significantly lower in KCTD12b KO mice compared with WT, KCTD8 KO, and KCTD8/12b KO mice.
source: PPR was significantly lower in KCTD12b KO mice (1.22 ± 0.11, n = 24 cells) compared with WT (2.40 ± 0.31, n = 27 cells; p=0.0051, Kruskal–Wallis test), KCTD8 KO (2.26 ± 0.27, n = 17 cells; p=0.0080), and KCTD8/12b KO mice (2.76 ± 0.37, n = 11 cells; p=0.0010).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's paired-pulse ratio measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Application of 1 µM baclofen potentiates EPSC amplitudes in all KCTD KO lines with similar intensities.
source: In contrast to these changes in basal release, application of 1 µM baclofen still potentiated EPSC amplitudes in all KCTD KO lines with similar intensities (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; WT: 615.1 ± 148.9% of baseline; n = 13; KCTD8 KO: 470.8 ± 73.5%; n = 9; KCTD12b KO: 485.4 ± 146.6%; n = 12; KCTD8/12b double KO: 445.8 ± 76.2%; n = 10; F4, 51 = 0.4723, p=0.7558, one-way ANOVA), suggesting that KCTDs are not involved in the GBR-mediated enhancement of EPSC amplitudes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's baclofen application data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: KCTDs are not involved in the GBR-mediated enhancement of EPSC amplitudes.
source: In contrast to these changes in basal release, application of 1 µM baclofen still potentiated EPSC amplitudes in all KCTD KO lines with similar intensities (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; WT: 615.1 ± 148.9% of baseline; n = 13; KCTD8 KO: 470.8 ± 73.5%; n = 9; KCTD12b KO: 485.4 ± 146.6%; n = 12; KCTD8/12b double KO: 445.8 ± 76.2%; n = 10; F4, 51 = 0.4723, p=0.7558, one-way ANOVA), suggesting that KCTDs are not involved in the GBR-mediated enhancement of EPSC amplitudes.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the similar baclofen effects across all KCTD KO lines.

claim: The release probability from ventral MHb terminals of KCTD12b KO mice is significantly increased compared with WT mice.
source: Compared with WT mice (WT release probability: 0.26 ± 0.04, n = 16 cells), the release probability from ventral MHb terminals of KCTD12b KO mice (0.49 ± 0.05, n = 9 cells) was significantly increased (Figure 6E; F2, 34 = 21.23, p<0.0001; WT vs. KCTD12b KO: p=0.0005, one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's variance-mean analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The release probability in KCTD8 KO mice is significantly lower than that of WT or KCTD12b KO mice.
source: In contrast, the release probability in KCTD8 KO mice (0.12 ± 0.02, n = 12 cells) was significantly lower than that of WT or KCTD12b KO mice (WT vs. KCTD8 KO: p=0.0176; KCTD8 KO vs. KCTD12b KO: p<0.0001; Tukey post hoc test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's variance-mean analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The quantal size remains unaffected by genotype in KCTD KO mice.
source: The quantal size remained unaffected by genotype (F2, 34 = 1.613, p=0.2142).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's variance-mean analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Overexpression of KCTD8 in WT mice results in significantly lower PPR values compared with EGFP controls.
source: PPR values recorded in rostral IPN neurons of EGFP control-injected animals remained unchanged (LV-EGFP: 2.17 ± 0.18, n = 17, five mice), whereas KCTD8-injected animals exhibited significantly lower PPR values (LV-KCTD8: 1.41 ± 0.14, n = 13, three mice; t28 = 3.20, p=0.0034; unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's lentiviral overexpression data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Lentiviral expression of KCTD12b in KCTD12b KO mice significantly increases PPR values compared with EGFP control-injected mice.
source: In contrast, lentiviral expression of KCTD12b in KCTD12b KO mice significantly increased PPR values compared with EGFP control-injected mice (Figure 6G; KCTD12b KO EGFP Control: 1.38 ± 0.09, n = 11, three mice; PPR KCTD12b KO rescue: 2.18 ± 0.29, n = 14, three mice; t23 = 2.98, p=0.0068, unpaired t-test), resulting in PPR values not significantly different from those of WT mice (WT LV-EGFP vs. KCTD12b rescue: t29 = 0.40, p=0.6925, unpaired t-test), confirming that the reduced PPR in KCTD12b KO mice is due to the lack of KCTD12b and not caused by developmental alterations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's lentiviral rescue data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The reduced PPR in KCTD12b KO mice is due to the lack of KCTD12b and not caused by developmental alterations.
source: In contrast, lentiviral expression of KCTD12b in KCTD12b KO mice significantly increased PPR values compared with EGFP control-injected mice (Figure 6G; KCTD12b KO EGFP Control: 1.38 ± 0.09, n = 11, three mice; PPR KCTD12b KO rescue: 2.18 ± 0.29, n = 14, three mice; t23 = 2.98, p=0.0068, unpaired t-test), resulting in PPR values not significantly different from those of WT mice (WT LV-EGFP vs. KCTD12b rescue: t29 = 0.40, p=0.6925, unpaired t-test), confirming that the reduced PPR in KCTD12b KO mice is due to the lack of KCTD12b and not caused by developmental alterations.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the rescue of PPR by lentiviral KCTD12b expression.

claim: KCTDs differentially modulate basal release probability at ventral MHb terminals.
source: Overall, these results show that KCTDs differentially modulate basal release probability at ventral MHb terminals.
evidence: This claim is a summary inference based on the combined results from KCTD KO mice and overexpression experiments.

claim: The increase in Cav2.3-mediated release probability by KCTD8 is consistent with its facilitatory effects on Cav2.3 current density in HEK293 cells.
source: The increase in Cav2.3-mediated release probability by KCTD8 is consistent with its facilitatory effects on Cav2.3 current density in HEK293 cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference connecting the in vitro and in vivo findings.

claim: There is no significant difference in the densities of Cav2.3 in the presynaptic active zone in the rostral relative to the lateral IPN between WT and KCTD12b KO mice.
source: We found no significant difference in the densities of Cav2.3 in the presynaptic active zone in the rostral relative to the lateral IPN (Figure 7B; WT rostral: 1.01 ± 0.04 fold of lateral IPN, n = 8 replicas from eight mice; KCTD12b KO: 1.06 ± 0.13 fold of lateral IPN, n = 8 replicas from eight mice; p=0.5054, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's SDS-FRL quantification data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The relative density of KCTD8 in the active zone of MHb terminals is increased approximately twofold in KCTD12b KO mice compared with WT mice.
source: Interestingly, the relative density of KCTD8 in the active zone of MHb terminals was increased approximately twofold in KCTD12b KO mice compared with those of WT mice (Figure 7B; WT rostral: 0.84 ± 0.12 fold of lateral IPN, n = 5 replicas from five mice; KCTD12b KO: 2.09 ± 0.45 fold of lateral IPN, n = 5 replicas from five mice; p=0.0079, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's SDS-FRL quantification data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The increased release probability in KCTD12b KO mice could be ascribable to a compensatory increase of KCTD8 in the active zone resulting in enhanced association of KCTD8 with Cav2.3.
source: This result indicates that the increased release probability in KCTD12b KO mice could be ascribable to a compensatory increase of KCTD8 in the active zone resulting in enhanced association of KCTD8 with Cav2.3.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the increased KCTD8 density in the active zone of KCTD12b KO mice.

claim: GABAB1 expression in the presynaptic active zone of MHb terminals is not significantly different between WT and KCTD12b KO.
source: On the other hand, GABAB1 expression in the presynaptic active zone of MHb terminals was not significantly different between WT and KCTD12b KO (Figure 7B; WT rostral: 1.30 ± 0.18 fold of lateral IPN, n = 3 replicas from three mice; KCTD12b KO: 0.89 ± 0.07 fold of lateral IPN, n = 3 replicas from three mice; p=0.4000, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's SDS-FRL quantification data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The density of KCTD8 particles in the active zone of rostral IPN synapses is significantly increased compared with lateral IPN synapses in KCTD12b KO mice.
source: The distribution pattern of KCTD8 in the lateral IPN showed peak densities in the peri-synaptic region, as seen in WT (Figure 3C). In contrast, the density of KCTD8 particles in the active zone, but not in the peri- or extrasynaptic area of rostral IPN synapses was significantly increased compared with lateral IPN synapses (main effect of presynaptic distribution: F4, 775 = 31.65, p<0.0001; rostral active zone vs. lateral active zone: p<0.0001; two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc test), showing an altered distribution pattern (compare with Figure 3C,F) and similar to that of Cav2.3 and KCTD12b in WT animals (Figure 3A,E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's pre-embedding immunogold labeling data in KCTD12b KO mice shown in Figure 7C.

claim: KCTD8 compensates for the loss of KCTD12b in the active zone of ventral MHb terminals.
source: This observation confirmed that KCTD8 compensates for the loss of KCTD12b in the active zone of ventral MHb terminals.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the altered distribution of KCTD8 in KCTD12b KO mice.

claim: Pre-incubation with anti-KCTD8 antibody significantly reduces Cav2.3 labeling densities in the active zone of rostral IPN synapses in KCTD12b KO mice.
source: In rostral IPN synapses, we found that the pre-incubation significantly reduced Cav2.3 labeling densities in the active zone, but not the peri- or extrasynaptic regions (Figure 7D; main effect of synaptic distribution: F4, 880 = 31.42, p<0.0001; control active zone vs. pre-incubation active zone: p=0.0006; two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's steric hindrance experiment data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Pre-incubation with anti-KCTD8 antibody slightly but significantly reduces Cav2.3 labeling density only in the peri-synaptic region of lateral IPN synapses.
source: In the lateral IPN, pre-incubation slightly but significantly reduced Cav2.3 labeling density only in the peri-synaptic region (Figure 7E; main effect of synaptic distribution: F4, 890 = 39.01; control <50 nm vs. pre-incubation <50 nm: p=0.0320).
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's steric hindrance experiment data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The peri-synaptic region is the location exhibiting peak expression for KCTD8 in dorsal MHb terminals.
source: The peri-synaptic region is the location exhibiting peak expression for KCTD8 in dorsal MHb terminals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the pre-embedding immunogold labeling data.

claim: The significant reduction in Cav2.3 labeling density at the peri-synaptic position validates the steric hindrance approach.
source: The peri-synaptic region is the location exhibiting peak expression for KCTD8 in dorsal MHb terminals. The significant reduction in Cav2.3 labeling density at this position therefore validates our steric hindrance approach.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the correlation between KCTD8 localization and the effect of steric hindrance.

claim: KCTDs in the active zone dynamically regulate the release probability, which may be important for scaling synaptic strength independent from GBRs in the MHb-IPN pathway.
source: These results support that KCTDs in the active zone dynamically regulate the release probability, which may be important for scaling synaptic strength independent from GBRs in the MHb-IPN pathway.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined results showing KCTD modulation of release and compensatory mechanisms.

claim: The active zone of ventral MHb terminals predominantly contains Cav2.3 and KCTD12b in WT mice.
source: In summary, the active zone of ventral MHb terminals predominantly contains Cav2.3 and KCTD12b, whereas the peri-synaptic region exhibits high levels of KCTD8 and GBRs (Figure 8, WT terminal).
evidence: This claim is a summary of the manuscript's electron microscopy findings shown in Figure 8.

claim: The peri-synaptic region of ventral MHb terminals exhibits high levels of KCTD8 and GBRs in WT mice.
source: In summary, the active zone of ventral MHb terminals predominantly contains Cav2.3 and KCTD12b, whereas the peri-synaptic region exhibits high levels of KCTD8 and GBRs (Figure 8, WT terminal).
evidence: This claim is a summary of the manuscript's electron microscopy findings shown in Figure 8.

claim: In the absence of KCTD12b, KCTD8 enters the active zone to interact with Cav2.3, thereby increasing Ca2+ influx and ultimately release.
source: In the absence of KCTD12b, KCTD8 enters the active zone to interact with Cav2.3, thereby increasing Ca2+ influx and ultimately release (Figure 8, KCTD12b KO terminal).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined results from KCTD12b KO mice shown in Figure 8.

claim: Cav2.3 is involved in mediating transmitter release at both the ventral and dorsal MHb-IPN pathways.
source: We confirmed that Cav2.3 is involved in mediating transmitter release at both pathways, but only release at the ventral MHb-IPN pathway exclusively relies on Cav2.3.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's electrophysiology data showing SNX-482 effects in both pathways.

claim: Only release at the ventral MHb-IPN pathway exclusively relies on Cav2.3.
source: We confirmed that Cav2.3 is involved in mediating transmitter release at both pathways, but only release at the ventral MHb-IPN pathway exclusively relies on Cav2.3.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's electrophysiology data in Cav2.3 KO mice.

claim: KCTD8 and KCTD12b show distinct expression along the MHb-IPN pathways.
source: KCTD8 and KCTD12b show distinct expression along these pathways, with KCTD12b specifically expressed in the cholinergic ventral MHb-IPN pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's immunofluorescence data.

claim: KCTD12b is specifically expressed in the cholinergic ventral MHb-IPN pathway.
source: KCTD8 and KCTD12b show distinct expression along these pathways, with KCTD12b specifically expressed in the cholinergic ventral MHb-IPN pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's immunofluorescence data.

claim: KCTD8 increases basal release probability at ventral MHb terminals.
source: Genetic deletion of the KCTDs indicated that KCTD8 increases basal release probability and that KCTD12b prevents this effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's variance-mean analysis and overexpression experiments.

claim: KCTD12b prevents the increase in basal release probability by KCTD8.
source: Genetic deletion of the KCTDs indicated that KCTD8 increases basal release probability and that KCTD12b prevents this effect.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the increased release probability in KCTD12b KO mice and the compensatory increase of KCTD8.

claim: Neither P/Q- nor N-type Ca2+ channels are expressed in MHb neurons.
source: In contrast to other brain areas, R-type Ca2+ channels may be the exclusive source of presynaptic Ca2+ influx to trigger release from ventral MHb terminals, given that neither P/Q- nor N-type Ca2+ channels are expressed in MHb neurons (Ludwig et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: R-type Ca2+ channels may be the exclusive source of presynaptic Ca2+ influx to trigger release from ventral MHb terminals.
source: In contrast to other brain areas, R-type Ca2+ channels may be the exclusive source of presynaptic Ca2+ influx to trigger release from ventral MHb terminals, given that neither P/Q- nor N-type Ca2+ channels are expressed in MHb neurons (Ludwig et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the absence of other Ca2+ channel types and the manuscript's functional data.

claim: The Allen Brain Atlas shows no expression of Cav2.1 and Cav2.2 in MHb neurons.
source: The finding by Ludwig et al., 1997 fits the data of the Allen Brain Atlas, which shows no expression of Cav2.1 and Cav2.2 in MHb neurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 1; images from Allen Institute for Brain Science, 2004) (Lein et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the Allen Brain Atlas data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The predominant presynaptic localization of Cav2.3 immunoreactivity was previously reported.
source: Although the predominant presynaptic localization of Cav2.3 immunoreactivity was previously reported (Parajuli et al., 2012), the functional implications of this localization were not determined.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The functional implications of the predominant presynaptic localization of Cav2.3 were not determined prior to this study.
source: Although the predominant presynaptic localization of Cav2.3 immunoreactivity was previously reported (Parajuli et al., 2012), the functional implications of this localization were not determined.
evidence: This claim is supported by the lack of prior functional studies on this topic.

claim: The remaining release from dorsal MHb terminals in the lateral IPN of Cav2.3 KO mice could be explained by compensatory upregulation of other Ca2+ channels or by the presence of additional Ca2+ channels in WT mice.
